newsitem.title: USA: U.S. permits new ASCAP European royalties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. permits new ASCAP European royalties.

text.p: The American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers (ASCAP) has won the right to collect royalties for home taping of copyright music in Canada, France and Germany, the federal government announced Wednesday. ASCAP licenses and collects fees for the use of music

written and published by its members. Under a 1992 U.S. Law, companies making tape machines or blank tapes pay money into a fund for each sale, on the theory that some blank tapes will be used by consumers to record copyright music for their own use.
But ASCAP has been barred from making similar arrangements in other countries because of a 1950 agreement between the government and ASCAP.
That 1950 decree -- made decades before home taping was on the horizon as a legal issue -- settled a complaint that ASCAP had violated antitrust laws by dividing up the markets in foreign countries.

"At the time the settlement was entered, ASCAP participated in a worldwide confederation of performing rights societies that engaged in global misconduct," said Assistant Attorney General Joel Klein, who heads the antitrust division.
Klein said all that has changed and that the old agreement was "affect(ing) American music rights-holders' ability to receive royalties for the foreign use of their work."
Consequently, Klein agreed to modify the provision.
